q: You must back up a server's configuration. Which folder matters most?
explain: /etc holds config, /var changing data (logs, databases), /home the users. Keeping /etc in git (etckeeper) helps.

q: An app misbehaves. Where do you look first?
choices: Its config in /etc, to rewrite it
explain: Read the error before changing anything: the log usually names the file or setting at fault.

q: Why work as your own user with sudo rather than logged in as root?
choices: Fewer accidents, and each sudo is logged with your name
explain: root (UID 0) can do everything; sudo gives it for one command, and leaves a trace of who did what.

q: A server is slow. Which command shows what eats the CPU right now?
explain: top (or htop) sorts live by CPU; M sorts by memory. ps aux is a snapshot, handy in scripts.

q: How do you see who logged in to a server recently, and from where?
explain: last reads the login records: user, source address, time. who shows who is logged in right now.

q: Writes fail with 'No space left on device'. What do you check first?
explain: df = disk free, per filesystem. Then du -sh /var/* finds the folder that grew (often logs).

q: free -h shows little 'free' memory but a lot 'available'. Is RAM short?
choices: No: spare RAM serves as cache and is given back
explain: Linux fills idle RAM with file cache. 'available' is what programs can still get.

q: `ls -l` shows -rw-r--r-- on a file. Who can change it?
explain: Three blocks: owner, group, others; r read, w write, x run. That is chmod 644.

q: A file with a database password is -rw-r--r--. What is wrong?
choices: Every user on the machine can read it
explain: chmod 600 keeps it to its owner. SSH even refuses private keys that others can read.

q: What is ~/.ssh/authorized_keys?
choices: The public keys allowed to log in as you
explain: One key per line. An unknown line there is a door someone left open: check it.

q: A process ignores Ctrl+C. What do you try before kill -9?
choices: kill PID, which lets it clean up
explain: kill sends TERM (15), which it can handle; KILL (9) can't be caught: no cleanup, half-written files.

q: You restart a web app and want to watch its log live. What do you run?
explain: Ctrl+C stops following. journalctl -fu app does the same for a systemd service.

q: You change who may use sudo. Why edit with visudo?
choices: It checks the syntax: a typo could lock everyone out of sudo
explain: Better still, add a file in /etc/sudoers.d/ with visudo -f, and keep a root shell open while testing.

q: Where do you see failed SSH logins?
choices: journalctl -u ssh, or the auth log in /var/log
explain: Hundreds of failures from one address = brute force; fail2ban or keys-only logins stop it. Rocky logs to /var/log/secure.

q: `ls -l` shows -rwsr-xr-x root on a program. What does the s mean?
choices: It runs as root, whoever starts it
explain: SUID. passwd needs it; an unexpected one is a red flag. find / -perm -4000 lists them all.

q: You added a disk to /etc/fstab. How do you test it before rebooting?
explain: A bad fstab line can stop the boot. mount -a (or findmnt --verify) shows the mistake while you can still fix it.

q: `ss -tlnp` shows 0.0.0.0:5432 for postgres. What does it mean?
choices: It listens on every interface, reachable from outside
explain: 127.0.0.1:5432 would be local only. Listen only where needed and firewall the rest.

q: df -h shows free space, yet you get 'No space left on device'. What else can be full?
explain: Each file takes an inode; millions of tiny files (sessions, cache) use them up before the space.

q: You deleted a huge log, but df shows no space back. Why?
choices: A process still has it open
explain: lsof +L1 lists deleted files still open. Restart that process; next time empty a log with `> file`, not rm.

q: What is the difference between a hard and a soft link?
choices: A soft link points to a path, a hard link to the inode
explain: Delete the target and a soft link breaks, a hard link doesn't.

q: A script works by hand but fails from cron. Most likely cause?
choices: cron runs it with a tiny PATH and environment
explain: Use full paths or set PATH in the crontab, and log the output (>> file 2>&1) to see the error.

q: A backup script logs in to a server by SSH. Which key should it use?
choices: Its own key, limited to that job in authorized_keys
root's key, copied to each server
One passphrase-less key shared by all scripts
explain: One key per job: you can revoke it alone, and command="…", from="…" restrict what it may do.

q: What is /etc/passwd for?
choices: The list of accounts: name, id, home and shell
The list of groups on the machine
The list of users logged in right now
explain: One line per account: name:x:uid:gid:comment:home:shell. No secret in it, which is why everyone can read it.

q: Where are the password hashes kept on a modern Linux?
explain: That is why /etc/passwd stays world-readable: it holds no secret.

q: In /etc/shadow, which second field means the account has a usable password?
explain: $y$ is yescrypt (today's default), $6$ SHA-512, $2b$ bcrypt. `!` and `*` block the password, empty means none.

q: You edited sshd_config on a remote server. What do you do before reloading sshd?
choices: sshd -t, and keep your current session open
explain: sshd -t checks the file. A broken config can lock you out: test a new login before closing the old one.

q: A process with a random name runs from /tmp. What do you do first?
choices: Note its binary and connections before killing it
explain: ls -l /proc/PID/exe and ss -p show what and who it talks to; killing it first destroys evidence. Then isolate the machine.

q: Which sshd setting stops password guessing altogether?
explain: A new port only cuts the noise in the logs; keys only removes the attack. Make sure your key works first.

q: What does `sudo -l` show?
choices: The commands you may run with sudo
The users in the sudo group
explain: Attackers run it first too: (ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/vim is root for anyone who knows :!sh.

q: What is /run for?
choices: Runtime files, in memory, emptied at each boot
explain: PID files and sockets live there; /var/run is a link to it.

q: What belongs in /usr/local?
choices: Software you installed outside the package manager
Local copies of the package cache
explain: The package manager owns /usr; /usr/local is yours.

q: Why send a server's logs to another machine as well?
choices: An intruder who gets root can erase the local ones
Logs are faster to write there
explain: rsyslog or systemd-journal-upload forward them; the copy elsewhere is what you read after an incident.
